# Crawl demand

*Metric*

How much Google wants to crawl a site's URLs, driven by their popularity and how often they change.

**Glossary** (*Crawl demand*): How much Google wants to crawl a site, driven by its quality, how often its URLs change and how popular they are. Demand from other Google products, such as Ads, counts too, a Google panelist said.

Narrative: the topics [Crawl demand](../topics/crawl-demand.md), [Crawl demand inherited by path](../topics/crawl-demand-inheritance.md) tell the story; this card lists what links to it.

15 claims mention it: 1 from Google's documentation, 11 shown or said at the event (2 not in Google docs, 1 confirmed by Google docs, 7 consistent with Google docs, 1 nothing to verify), 3 the author's analysis. A card is a map: cite the claim ids, with the citation given after each claim.

## Google's documentation

Documented in: [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget).

- [`D1-C132`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Docs: Google's crawl budget guide says each crawler has its own crawl demand, but the crawl capacity limit (hostload) is shared across all crawlers, so high demand from one crawler can reduce the capacity left for others. `[D1-C132, docs, Google, https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget]`

## Shown or said at the event

Not in Google's documentation first: present those as said at Search Central Live, never as documented policy.

- [`D1-C377`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Stage, Day 1, not in Google docs: The quality that drives crawl demand is the quality of the site as a whole, not the quality of an individual page. `[D1-C377, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D3-C622`](../sessions/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) Slide, Day 3, not in Google docs: Google estimated that a crawl demand update driven by Search takes about 20 hours on average, with a minimum of minutes and an end point of weeks to months. `[D3-C622, slide, Google, Day 3]`
- [`D1-C440`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, confirmed by Google docs: If a site's server cannot cope with the extra crawling that higher crawl demand brings, Google reduces its crawling of that site again. `[D1-C440, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C090`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Slide, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Crawl budget is the combination of crawl rate limit and crawl demand. `[D1-C090, slide, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C093`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Slide, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Crawl demand is driven by the quality of the site, the change frequency of its URLs and their popularity on the internet. `[D1-C093, slide, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C439`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Very large, constantly changing sites get no special handling: when URLs change frequently or are useful to users, Google raises crawl demand and tries to raise its crawl capacity for the site, the same logic it applies to small sites. `[D1-C439, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C493`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: There is no easy way to tell whether a drop in Google's crawling comes from lower crawl demand or a lower crawl capacity limit; most of the time a capacity-limit drop is an abrupt step down. `[D1-C493, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C538`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: A Google panelist said crawl demand is not only Search's: when enough of a site's URLs are wanted by Search, Google Ads or another Google product, Google raises the site's crawl demand and crawls up to that level of demand as far as the site's crawl capacity allows. `[D1-C538, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D3-C623`](../sessions/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) Stage, Day 3, consistent with Google docs: When Google notices the web getting excited about a few URLs on a site, it allocates more crawl demand to the whole site so it does not miss content useful to future searchers. `[D3-C623, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 3]`
- [`D3-C624`](../sessions/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) Stage, Day 3, consistent with Google docs: Crawl demand can also come from other Google products, such as Shopping, and the roughly 20-hour estimate covers only demand from Search. `[D3-C624, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 3]`
- [`D1-C545`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, nothing to verify: An audience member asked, for very large sites of about 100 million pages, what signs show that a site is limited by crawl budget, and how to tell a crawl capacity limit problem from a crawl demand problem. `[D1-C545, stage, an audience member, Day 1]`

## The author's analysis

- [`D1-C067`](../sessions/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) Analysis: A page with no internal links depends on sitemaps alone to be found, so it is discovered slowly and attracts little crawl demand. `[D1-C067, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D1-C095`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Analysis: New content inherits its starting crawl demand from the folder it sits in. Put new high-value content under sections Google already rates well, not under weak ones. `[D1-C095, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D1-C420`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Analysis: The stage remark that crawl demand follows the quality of the site as a whole sits beside the same talk's slide (D1-C094), which falls back to the parent path's aggregate only when a URL's own quality is unknown, and Google's crawl budget guide lists page quality among the demand factors; read it as site quality setting the baseline while known URL-level signals still count. `[D1-C420, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`

## For developers

- `DEV-PRF-01` **SHOULD** · Documented: Keep connect time and time to first byte low and stable under crawler load (3 of its claims mention it)
- `DEV-URL-04` **MUST** · Documented: Link every indexable page from the normal navigation or a hub page (1 of its claims mentions it; its own text names it)
- `DEV-URL-10` **SHOULD** · Said at Search Central Live: Group URLs into meaningful section paths and launch new content under sections Google already indexes well (1 of its claims mentions it; its own text names it)
